tagline: A river of rainforest at Africa's heart
overview:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is the second-largest country in Africa and about one-quarter the size of the United States, so large that it spans two time zones. It lies in the center of the continent, mostly covered by the Congo rainforest, the second-largest tropical forest on Earth after the Amazon. The capital, Kinshasa, on the Congo River, is one of the biggest cities in Africa with over 15 million people. The country borders nine nations and has only a tiny sliver of Atlantic coast.

Around 100 million people live in the DR Congo, making it the most populous French-speaking country in the world. French is the official language, and Lingala, Kikongo, Swahili, and Tshiluba are national languages among more than 200 spoken. The country is a republic with an elected president. Beneath its soil lie some of the world's greatest reserves of copper, cobalt, diamonds, and gold, yet most people remain poor, and armed conflict has troubled the east for decades. Congolese music and dance, meanwhile, are loved across the whole continent.
landAndNature: The Congo River, second in the world by water volume, loops through the country in a giant arc, collecting hundreds of tributaries and crossing the equator twice. A vast basin of rainforest fills the center, with hardwood trees, orchids, and river villages reachable only by boat. To the east rise the mountains of the Albertine Rift, including the snowcapped Rwenzori and the Virunga volcanoes, where Nyiragongo holds one of the world's largest lava lakes. Virunga National Park, Africa's oldest, shelters mountain gorillas. The DR Congo is the only home of the bonobo, the okapi, a shy forest relative of the giraffe with zebra-striped legs, and the Congo peafowl. Elephants, chimpanzees, and hippos also live here, and Lake Tanganyika forms part of the eastern border.
peopleAndCulture: The Congolese belong to hundreds of ethnic groups, among them the Luba, Kongo, Mongo, and Mangbetu, and most are Christian. Cassava is the staple, cooked into fufu or leaves pounded into pondu, with grilled fish, chicken in peanut sauce, and plantains. Kinshasa is Africa's music capital: Congolese rumba and its faster child, soukous, with sparkling guitar lines, are danced from Dakar to Nairobi, and stars like Franco and Papa Wemba became legends. Sapeurs dress in flamboyant suits as a statement of pride. Soccer is the top sport, and Congolese-born players star in European leagues. Congolese painters and sculptors, from Mangbetu carvers to modern artists like Chéri Samba, are collected worldwide.
history: Bantu-speaking peoples built kingdoms such as Kongo, Luba, and Kuba in the centuries before Europeans arrived. In 1885 King Leopold II of Belgium took the entire Congo basin as his personal property and forced people to gather rubber and ivory under brutal conditions; millions died before Belgium took over as a colony in 1908. Independence came on June 30, 1960, but the first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was murdered within months. Army officer Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire, and ruled as a dictator until 1997. Wars from 1996 to 2003 drew in neighboring countries and cost millions of lives, and fighting by armed groups continues in the east. The first peaceful transfer of power through elections came in 2019.
funFacts: The Congo River is so deep, over 220 meters in places, that it is the deepest river in the world.
Bonobos, one of humans' closest relatives, live only in the forests south of the Congo River and nowhere else on Earth.
The okapi has zebra-striped legs, a giraffe's long tongue, and was unknown to science until 1901.
The country's cobalt mines supply most of the metal used in the batteries of phones and electric cars.
Kinshasa and Brazzaville, capitals of two different countries, face each other across the Congo River, close enough to see.
